analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits and applies the payroll tax to all earnings above the cap.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced in August 2021 and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill raises Social Security benefits for lower- and middle-income retirees and disabled workers by paying a higher share of the first dollars a worker earned, and by increasing the dollar amount of earnings that gets the most generous treatment. It would compute annual cost-of-living increases using an index that tracks what older households actually buy, improve survivor benefits for widows and widowers in two-income households, and stop the increases from shrinking benefits for the poorest disabled recipients. It pays for this by phasing out the earnings cap on the Social Security payroll tax, so that by 2027 every dollar earned above roughly $143,000 is taxed at the full 12.4% rate.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future retirees and disabled workers, who would get larger checks, with the biggest percentage gains for those who earned less over their careers. Widows and widowers in two-income households would get a better benefit instead of being pushed onto the lower of the two earnings records. Recipients of Supplemental Security Income would be protected from having those increases clawed back.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirees, disabled workers, and surviving spouses

how_it_helps.text: Raises the share of the first dollars of earnings counted in the benefit formula from 90% to 95% (phased in from 2027 to 2030) and increases the dollar amount of earnings receiving that treatment by 1% a year up to 15%, lifting benefits most for lower- and middle-income retirees and disabled workers.

Switches Social Security cost-of-living increases to a new Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which tracks the spending of older households — including medical costs — and typically rises faster than the index used today.

For widows and widowers in two-income households, replaces the current rule (which generally gives the survivor only the larger of the two spouses' benefits) with the greater of the deceased spouse's benefit or 75% of the couple's combined benefit, so a surviving spouse does not have to live on one low earnings record.
Holds SSI beneficiaries harmless: the higher Social Security benefits cannot be counted as income in a way that reduces their Supplemental Security Income payments.

Pays for the expansion by phasing out the cap on earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax: in 2023 only 20% of earnings above the cap is taxable, rising each year until 2027, when all earnings above the cap are taxed at the full rate.

analysis.who_pays: People earning more than the payroll-tax cap — about $142,800 in 2022 — would pay the full 12.4% Social Security tax on every dollar above it once the phase-in completes in 2027, and high-earning self-employed people would pay both the employee and employer shares. They would get a small offset: 5% of their above-cap earnings would count toward their own future benefits.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners above the payroll-tax cap

drawbacks.text: The tax is substantial for top earners: a worker well above the cap would owe 12.4% on every dollar of wages above it each year, and self-employed professionals and business owners pay both halves, with only a partial offset (5% of surplus earnings counts toward their own benefit).

The benefit improvements phase in slowly: the higher 95% replacement rate is not fully in effect until 2030, the increased first bend point not until 2042, and the new benefit formulas apply only to people becoming eligible after 2027, so near-term retirees would mainly see the cost-of-living change.

A good-faith objection supporters would have to answer: removing the cap changes Social Security's financing, since high earners would pay the tax on income far beyond what is credited to their own benefit, and the switch to an elderly price index permanently raises program costs. This is the core trade-off the bill's sponsors accepted rather than a flaw in drafting.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains and costs are clearly aimed. The benefit increases are concentrated on people with lower lifetime earnings, older households' actual cost of living, and surviving spouses — while the cost falls almost entirely on households in roughly the top few percent of earners. The design is gradual, with the tax phase-in spread over 2023-2027 and benefit changes over 2027-2042, which limits disruption but also means the biggest benefit gains arrive late. The main honest trade-off is fairness to high earners, partially mitigated by the 5% benefit credit on surplus earnings.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means and Education and Labor committees on the day it was introduced, and neither committee held a hearing, markup, or vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Linda Sánchez introduced the bill on August 3, 2021, and it was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means and, in addition, the Committee on Education and Labor.
Ten House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
No further action was ever taken: the action history shows the introduction and committee referrals and nothing else through the end of the Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners above the payroll-tax cap are better off, because the tax on their income above roughly $143,000 was never enacted. Status quo Social Security financing and benefit levels continue, with trust-fund shortfall debates left unaddressed by this approach.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners above the payroll-tax cap

for.name: Rep. Linda Sánchez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited nine original cosponsors from the Progressive and Black and Hispanic caucuses' ranks.

for.name: 10 of 213 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none of them chaired the committees with jurisdiction over it.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on August 3, 2021 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

against.name: Rep. Bobby Scott
against.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee was the second referee of the bill and also took no action on it during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All ten cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported it, but the bill never reached a floor vote, so there is no roll-call record; it died in committees controlled by the Democratic majority.

industries.note: The bill phases in the full 12.4% payroll tax on all earnings above the cap by 2027, ending the current exemption for income above roughly $143,000. Their gain in avoiding the tax came at the cost of the benefit expansions the bill would have funded for retirees.
High-earning self-employed people would pay both the employee and employer shares of the payroll tax on income above the cap, roughly 12.4% of the excess, with only a small benefit credit in return.
